chapter: Other Philadelphia work and the union
title: Leaving Charlie Miller for Boston and losing touch
summary: Miller's was the last band he played before going to school in Boston. Waters admits he stays out of touch with old friends, and notes Miller later headed a Black musicians' local in Albany.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Did you work with Charlie Miller's Orchestra right up to the point when you departed for -
Yes, that was the last any kind of band that I worked with. That was the last any type of -
What did you do, give them your notice, said 'I'm going to go to school in Boston?'
Right. And did you stay in contact with any of your Philadelphia musical friends?
No, now that's something, that's my fault there, that's something that I still have got to learn to do, (laughs) to stay in contact with people. That's one of my biggest

faults, I mean, that is bad for me too, you know. I don't stay in contact enough, 'cause they were a great gang, that gang. If I'd stayed in contact I could tell you more, see. Or I know that [ ] was from Buffalo, New York. And Bill - where he was born I don't know, but he came up 'round Philadelphia, see. And Ruth Marsee [?] the girl also came up 'round Phil, so where they born, I don't know. And Charlie Miller, see, in the end he turned out to be the president of an Albany musicians' local, negro - at the end, see, you know.
PS: Maybe we should ask Franc Williams, who spent some time in Albany in the '30s, if he knows Charlie Miller -
He should, yeah - yeah, yeah. Charlie Miller, that's the name. That's obviously Charlie Miller's name.
Did you ever see any of them ever again?
Never did. See, because I didn't stay there, see. I, when I left -
